prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: helping users manage privacy risks in voluntary online self-disclosure. The work combines dataset creation, span-level identification, a formative user study, and a new generation task for “abstraction” of disclosures. The topic is timely, societally relevant, and well aligned with current interest in privacy-aware NLP and human-centered language technologies. I found the paper ambitious and interesting, especially because it goes beyond standard detection benchmarks and attempts to connect modeling with actual user needs. At the same time, several aspects of the empirical methodology and evaluation leave me uncertain about the strength of the conclusions. Overall, I view the paper as promising and potentially impactful, but not yet fully convincing in its current form.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem framing. Much prior work on privacy in NLP focuses either on PII detection/redaction or on privacy leakage from models themselves. This paper instead focuses on user-side assistance for self-disclosure management, which is a meaningful distinction. The span-level formulation is also well motivated: if the goal is to help users decide what to revise, sentence-level labels are too coarse. The proposed taxonomy of 19 categories is another useful contribution, as it broadens the notion of privacy-relevant disclosure beyond canonical PII. The inclusion of both “attributes” and “experiences” is sensible and likely useful for downstream tools.

The dataset contribution appears valuable. A corpus of 2.4K Reddit posts with 4.8K annotated disclosure spans across 19 categories could be a useful resource for the community. The paper also makes some thoughtful annotation choices, such as preferring contextualized spans (“I live in the US”) over minimal spans (“US”), which is appropriate for user-facing highlighting. The use of in-house annotators and iterative quality control is also a positive sign. However, the paper does not provide enough annotation statistics to assess reliability. I would expect inter-annotator agreement for both the initial disclosure filtering stage and the span/category annotation stage, ideally before adjudication. Given that the user study later reveals substantial disagreement between annotators and end users about what counts as risky, agreement numbers are especially important here. Without them, it is hard to know whether the task itself is stable enough to support the reported modeling claims.

The identification experiments are reasonable but somewhat underdeveloped. Fine-tuning RoBERTa-large for token tagging is a sensible baseline, and the comparison across segmentation strategies is useful. The finding that sentence-level segmentation works best is plausible and practically relevant. The reported token-level F1 above 75% is encouraging. That said, the span-level F1 is much lower, around 49 for multiclass and 54 for binary in the best setting, which is a more realistic measure for a user-facing highlighting tool. Since the paper’s motivating use case depends on accurately identifying actionable spans, I think the paper should foreground span-level performance more than token-level performance. As written, the abstract and introduction emphasize “over 75% Token F1,” which risks overstating practical readiness.

The per-class results also reveal substantial unevenness. Some categories such as Age and Location are handled fairly well, while others such as Sexual Orientation and Relationship Status are much weaker. This matters because the lower-performing categories may be among the most sensitive. The paper acknowledges class imbalance and uses external tools for Name and Contact, but the hybrid system design is not evaluated in a fully integrated way. It is unclear what the end-to-end user-facing performance would be when combining the RoBERTa tagger, the sentence classifier, LUKE, and Presidio-based regexes. A complete system-level evaluation would strengthen the practical claims considerably.

A broader concern is the absence of stronger baselines and ablations for identification. The paper compares only variants of the same RoBERTa setup under different segmentation schemes. There is little sense of how difficult the task is relative to simpler alternatives or more modern sequence labeling approaches. For example, comparisons to CRF-based decoding, instruction-tuned LLM tagging, or even a sentence-classification-plus-span-extraction pipeline would help contextualize the results. Likewise, the contribution of the contextualized-span annotation policy is not empirically examined. Since the paper argues that this choice is important, it would be useful to show whether it improves user utility or model learnability.

The user study is a distinctive and commendable component. It is refreshing to see a privacy/NLP paper engage directly with users rather than relying solely on benchmark metrics. The qualitative findings are interesting: users appreciate the concept, but want personalization, subreddit awareness, and explanations; some perceive the model as oversensitive; and some explicitly ask for rewriting assistance. These observations are valuable and plausibly motivate the abstraction task. However, the study design also raises questions. The sample size is small (21 participants), which is acceptable for formative HCI work, but the paper mixes qualitative insights with quantitative summaries such as “82% positive outlook” and “62% would use it” in a way that may overstate generalizability. More importantly, the model outputs shown to participants were “manually annotated images” of detected spans. It is not fully clear whether participants saw raw model predictions, post-processed outputs, or researcher-curated visualizations. Since the study is used to support claims about real-world applicability, the exact presentation pipeline matters.

The abstraction task is novel and potentially impactful, but this section is also where I have the most reservations. The idea of replacing a disclosure with a less specific but still useful alternative is compelling and clearly distinct from standard redaction. The examples are intuitive, and the focus on span-level rewriting that must fit back into the original sentence is well chosen. However, the data creation and evaluation methodology make it difficult to assess whether the reported results demonstrate genuine progress.

The main issue is that the abstraction training and evaluation data are generated by LLMs rather than humans: ChatGPT for train/dev and GPT-4 for test references. This creates several problems. First, the task may become one of imitating another model’s stylistic preferences rather than learning a human-grounded notion of privacy-preserving abstraction. Second, automatic overlap metrics against GPT-4 references are of limited meaning, especially for a highly open-ended generation task with many valid outputs. Third, because the best-performing model is “distilled on GPT-4 generated abstractions,” the evaluation risks rewarding closeness to the teacher model rather than usefulness to users. The paper partly mitigates this with human evaluation, but even there the setup is limited.

The human evaluation for abstraction is not yet rigorous enough for strong claims. One author conducts the evaluation on 60 sampled instances using Rank & Rate, and then a second round compares the top two models on Likert scales. Having a single evaluator is a major weakness for a subjective task involving privacy reduction, utility preservation, diversity, and coherence. Inter-rater reliability is absent, and the paper does not explain whether the evaluator was blinded to system identity or hypotheses. Since the reported differences between methods are fairly small, this matters a lot. Also, the privacy score of the best model is only 3.19/5, which the authors appropriately describe as moderate, but this should temper the overall framing. The system seems better at producing diverse and coherent paraphrases than at substantially reducing privacy risk.

I also worry that the abstraction task lacks a clear operational definition of “privacy reduction.” In some cases, replacing a specific disclosure with a more general one may still leave highly identifying information when combined with context. In other cases, abstraction may preserve semantics but fail to reduce inferential privacy risk. The paper does not attempt any adversarial or inference-based evaluation, such as whether humans or models can still recover sensitive attributes from the abstracted text. Given the privacy motivation, such an evaluation would be much more compelling than lexical overlap or subjective Likert judgments alone. Even a small study measuring attribute inference before and after abstraction would significantly strengthen the claims.

Another conceptual issue is that the paper sometimes conflates “self-disclosure” with “privacy risk.” The user study itself shows that not all disclosures are perceived as risky, and risk depends on context, norms, audience, and user intent. The current models detect disclosures, not privacy harms. This distinction should be made more explicit throughout. Otherwise, there is a danger of presenting overinclusive detection as privacy protection. The paper does acknowledge oversensitivity and personalization as limitations, but these are central rather than peripheral issues.

The ethics discussion is thoughtful in some respects, especially around annotator protection and restricted release. Still, one statement gave me pause: the claim that model failures “do not pose additional risks” because they tend toward overprotection. I do not think this is fully justified. False negatives clearly pose risk by failing to warn users. False positives can also cause harm by nudging users away from beneficial self-expression, especially for marginalized communities whose identity disclosures may be important for support-seeking. Similarly, abstraction suggestions could inadvertently distort meaning or encourage deceptive self-presentation. The ethics section should engage more seriously with these possibilities.

There are also several missing experimental details that should be clarified. For the identification model, I could not find enough information about hyperparameters, training epochs, selection criteria, or variance across runs. For the abstraction models, the exact base model variant, LoRA configuration, decoding parameters, and prompt templates are only partially described. Since the paper compares many formatting/training variants with relatively small differences, reproducibility details are important. The paper would also benefit from confidence intervals or standard deviations, especially for the user study summaries and human evaluation results.

In terms of writing and presentation, the paper is generally understandable and the motivation is strong, but there are many grammatical errors and typos throughout. Examples include subject-verb agreement issues, inconsistent terminology, and awkward phrasing. These do not obscure the main ideas, but they do reduce polish. Some tables are also difficult to interpret. Table 5 in particular appears malformed in the provided text, and the ranking metric is not explained clearly enough. The paper would benefit from tighter editing and clearer presentation of the evaluation protocols.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has real merit. The combination of a new span-level taxonomy, a curated corpus, user-centered evaluation, and a novel abstraction task is ambitious and potentially influential. The work opens an interesting research direction at the intersection of privacy, NLP, and HCI. My hesitation is mainly about evidential strength: the identification results are promising but not yet strong enough for a robust user-facing tool, and the abstraction results rely too heavily on synthetic references and limited human evaluation.

To strengthen the paper, I would most strongly recommend the following. First, add annotation agreement statistics and more detail on adjudication. Second, provide a fuller end-to-end evaluation of the complete identification system, including Name/Contact handling. Third, include stronger baselines or at least more ablations for identification. Fourth, substantially improve the abstraction evaluation: use multiple human raters, report agreement, and if possible include a privacy-oriented downstream test such as attribute inference reduction before versus after abstraction. Fifth, clarify the distinction between detecting self-disclosure and assessing privacy risk, and moderate claims accordingly. Sixth, expand the discussion of harms from both false positives and false negatives.

My overall assessment is that this is a creative and important paper with promising early results, but the current empirical validation is not yet fully sufficient for the strength of its claims. I would be positive about this line of work and encourage revision, but for a top-tier ML venue I would lean borderline to weak reject unless the methodological gaps above are addressed.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies user-side privacy protection for online self-disclosures. It introduces a 19-category taxonomy of self-disclosure, a Reddit-based span-annotated corpus with 2.4K posts and 4.8K disclosure spans, and models for span-level identification and abstraction. For identification, the authors fine-tune RoBERTa-large for binary and multi-class tagging and report best token-level F1 above 75% (81.78% binary, 75.30% multi-class on sentence-level segmentation). They also supplement rare classes such as names/contact with external tools. A formative user study with 21 Reddit users suggests generally positive perceptions. Motivated by this, the paper proposes self-disclosure abstraction: rewriting disclosure spans to be less specific while preserving utility. Using Llama-2 fine-tuned on LLM-generated abstractions, the authors report moderate privacy reduction and high utility/diversity in human evaluation.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: protecting privacy at the point of user self-disclosure rather than only detecting PII or studying LM privacy leakage.
Introduces a reasonably broad taxonomy of 19 self-disclosure categories spanning both attributes and experiences, which is more fine-grained than much prior work.
Creates a span-level annotated corpus rather than only sentence/post labels, enabling more actionable detection and downstream rewriting.
Identification experiments are fairly comprehensive in terms of input segmentation choices and evaluation at token, partial-span, and exact-span levels.
The paper includes an HCI-oriented user study, which is valuable for grounding the task in real user needs and surfacing issues like personalization and subreddit context.
The abstraction task is novel and practically motivated; generating multiple candidate abstractions is a sensible design choice for user-facing systems.
Human evaluation for abstraction considers multiple dimensions beyond lexical overlap, including privacy reduction, utility, diversity, and coherence.
weaknesses: The empirical setup and reporting are incomplete in several important places, making it difficult to assess robustness and reproducibility.
The abstraction dataset is very small (159/25/50 posts for train/dev/test from the most recent 10% subset), yet the paper draws fairly broad conclusions about generation quality.

Ground-truth abstractions are generated by ChatGPT/GPT-4 rather than humans, so the task may largely measure imitation of proprietary LLM outputs rather than genuine privacy-preserving rewriting quality.
The user study is small (21 participants), qualitative, and uses manually annotated displays of model outputs, limiting claims about real-world effectiveness of an automated deployed system.
The paper does not provide inter-annotator agreement statistics for the main corpus or human evaluations, despite emphasizing annotation quality.

Rare but sensitive categories are effectively excluded from the main learned tagging model and handled by external tools/classifiers, which weakens the claim of a unified 19-category identification system.
The privacy benefit of abstraction is only described as moderate and is measured by subjective Likert ratings rather than any concrete adversarial or re-identification risk reduction metric.
There is little analysis of failure modes, subgroup effects, or category-specific harms, despite the privacy-sensitive application domain.
methodological_flaws: Selection bias in corpus construction: only posts that both initial annotators agreed contained disclosure were retained for span annotation. This removes hard negatives and borderline cases from the annotated corpus, likely inflating downstream performance and narrowing the operational definition of disclosure.

The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement (e.g., kappa/F1) for either the initial disclosure screening or the span/category annotations. Without reliability estimates, the validity of the taxonomy and labels is uncertain.

The test set appears to be formed from the two most recent batches with second-round annotation/adjudication, while train/val/test are also chronologically split. The exact relationship between adjudicated vs non-adjudicated data across splits is unclear, raising concerns about label quality mismatch between train and test.

For identification, the headline claim of broad 19-category coverage is not fully supported: name/contact are not learned in the same tagging framework but delegated to LUKE/Presidio plus a sentence classifier. This hybrid setup complicates evaluation and comparability, and no integrated end-to-end results over all 19 categories are reported.

The abstraction training/evaluation pipeline uses ChatGPT-generated references for train/dev and GPT-4-generated references for test. This introduces a distribution shift between training and testing references and makes automatic metrics difficult to interpret scientifically.

Automatic metrics for abstraction (BLEU/ROUGE) are weak proxies for privacy-preserving rewriting, especially when multiple valid abstractions exist. The paper acknowledges diversity but still relies heavily on overlap metrics without stronger task-specific evaluation.

Human evaluation for abstraction is conducted by one of the authors on 60 sampled instances according to the text. Single-annotator author evaluation is a serious validity concern due to bias and lack of reliability measurement.

Claims about privacy reduction are not substantiated by an objective threat model. No attacker-based evaluation, attribute inference reduction test, or re-identification analysis is provided, so the central privacy claim remains weakly validated.

The ethics statement claims model failures 'do not pose additional risks' and 'tend towards overprotection'; this is scientifically unsupported. False negatives clearly can fail to warn users, and poor abstractions could distort meaning or create misplaced trust.

The statement that no harms would disproportionately impact marginalized populations is not empirically justified, especially given that some categories (e.g., sexual orientation, mental health) are both sensitive and among the weaker-performing classes.
